title: I Wonder Who, the Laughin' Louie record and loose studio sessions
summary: They try to identify a tune from Laughin' Louie and discuss the humor and relaxed atmosphere of the sessions with Armstrong keeping everyone laughing.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: There was one tune that that band recorded, called 'I Wonder Who.' Do you remember that one?
'I Wonder Who.' Is that something about Somebody loves me, I wonder who?
No, not 'Somebody Loves Me.' It's just called 'I Wonder Who.' And there's no indication of who wrote the tune. I just thought you might recall.
'I Wonder Who.' This -- I mean, the band we're talking about now recorded it?
Yes.
Uh-huh.
Yeah, it was at the last session, in April, when you did 'Sweet Sue' and 'St. Louis Blues' and 'Don't Play Me Cheap' and 'Cabin in the Pines.' That was one of the tunes that you recorded then.
Uh-huh.
And it says, songwriter unknown. I thought you might recall. You did a tune called 'Laughin' Louis.'
Yes, 'Laughin' Louie.'
In which Louis --
That's right.
The band falls apart, and Louis says, watch out, cats, dig this. And plays some things. And then he plays a very lovely tune (musical sounds).
(Musical sounds.)
What is the name of that tune? People have been trying to find out for years. Do you know?
(Musical sounds.) Oh, what was that thing? You know, they played in there -- it was really pretty --
Beautiful.
It really was. And then, and when he made that run, Stump Whitlock said, change them, peewops, change them. You remember?
Yeah, yeah.
Yes, uh-huh.
But it sounds familiar to a lot of people, but nobody can come up with a name for it.
No. I don't know the name of that. It's a , I remember that. (Musical sounds.)
Then he said, -- there was this real pretty part, here.
Yes, that was really --
Beautiful, beautiful, unaccompanied thing. There's an awful lot of humor on those records, and a lot of talking

back and forth, and Louis would talk about people in the studios, like the Carpenter and Dunlop smoking the Louis Armstrong special cigar. I presume he meant cigar, he just said the Louis Armstrong Special. I don't know what --
(Laughter.)
Were they very loose affairs, the recording sessions?

Yes, they really was. Yes certainly -- you know, usually, recording sessions, you'd get tense, sometimes, when the red light -- especially when the red light come on. It'd be all right, long as you're just taking it down for the timing, and so, you'd say, all right, quiet, the red light come on and it looked like you were tensing up, sometimes. But, I don't know, Louis kept it going, he kept it funny, and you'd be laughing.
Those are really marvelous records.
Yeah.
